classification_signals: The thesis is based on five original articles (p. 10).
It includes three laboratory experiments (Studies I, II, III) and two field studies (Studies IV, V) (p. 4).
Study IV is described as a meta-analysis of individual participant data (p. 41).
Study V involves quasi-experimental before-after comparisons (p. 42).

limitations: Generalisability of laboratory results to real-life settings (p. 70).
Validity of experimental tasks, with effects only observed in short-term and working memory tasks, not complex tasks (p. 70).
Difficulty in developing realistic office tasks for repeated-measures designs (p. 71).
Laboratory participants were students, not office workers, potentially underestimating noise effects (p. 71).
Exclusion of individual differences (e.g., noise sensitivity) from the scope of research (p. 72).
Problematic falsifiability of the compensatory effort argument (p. 72).
STI calculation method is most appropriate for constant masking sounds (p. 72).
Distraction distance (rD) may have overestimated speech intelligibility in field studies due to assumptions of normal voice effort and lack of accounting for simultaneous speakers (p. 72).
Quality of experiments could have benefited from more pretesting and development of questionnaires and tasks (p. 72).
Ambitious individual experiment aims resulted in complex designs (p. 72).
minimum_safe_summary: This thesis investigates the impact of noise, particularly background speech, on cognitive performance and subjective reactions in open-plan offices, and explores design solutions. It finds that speech intelligibility (measured by STI) predicts subjective acoustic disturbance and impairs verbal short-term and working memory, but not more complex tasks. Increased office distractions mediate negative changes in environmental satisfaction, collaboration, and stress. Masking sounds, especially filtered pink noise and spring water, improve acoustic satisfaction, while music is not recommended. Holistic room acoustic design can reduce noise disturbance, though benefits are limited at short distances. Distraction distance (rD) predicts perceived noise disturbance. Providing easily accessible quiet workspaces is crucial for mitigating negative outcomes, especially for those with high concentration demands. Limitations include the generalisability of lab findings, the focus on basic memory tasks, and the retrospective design of field studies.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Irrelevant background speech acts as a distractor, creating a conflict between attending to the primary task and the distracting stimulus, leading to performance decrements.
Environmental stressors like noise increase cognitive load, thereby reducing the cognitive resources available for task performance, particularly for tasks requiring working memory.
Chronic exposure to noise in open-plan offices can lead to physiological and psychological stress responses, impacting well-being and cognitive function.

mechanism_chain.description: Background speech noise, particularly when intelligible, diverts attentional resources, increases cognitive load, and interferes with working memory processes, leading to impaired performance in tasks requiring verbal short-term memory.
